ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1).
table.formatted: For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1).

table.text: Unlike standard models in which a utility (or value) function and a noise term are fit by some form of a least squares procedure, to test our model we examine the error matrices produced by our subjects directly and compare them to the error matrices predicted by our theory.

If an experimentalist were to define 4 as the expected reference point when subjects were using this value function, they would observe a gain-loss asymmetry, a kind of loss aversion: If subjects were given a choice between $4 for sure or a 50/50 chance of either $3 or $5, they would prefer the $4 for sure.
Panel A: Empirical error matrices for the four subjects in the Uniform environment; color indicates the observed error rate, and numbers indicate the number of trials contributing to each cell.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1).

> Unlike standard models in which a utility (or value) function and a noise term are fit by some form of a least squares procedure, to test our model we examine the error matrices produced by our subjects directly and compare them to the error matrices predicted by our theory.

> If an experimentalist were to define 4 as the expected reference point when subjects were using this value function, they would observe a gain-loss asymmetry, a kind of loss aversion: If subjects were given a choice between $4 for sure or a 50/50 chance of either $3 or $5, they would prefer the $4 for sure.

> Panel A: Empirical error matrices for the four subjects in the Uniform environment; color indicates the observed error rate, and numbers indicate the number of trials contributing to each cell.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.

text.text: We thank all the members of the Glimcher and Tymula labs for their valuable discussions, constructive feedback, and support throughout the project.
We thank Dr.
In the mid-1600s, Blaise Pascal introduced the first mathematical framework for understanding human decision-making (Pascal, 1670).
text.formatted: In the mid-1600s, Blaise Pascal introduced the first mathematical framework for understanding human decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pascal, 1670)</ref>.

text.text: He emphasized the notion that humans ought to be acting in a way that rationally and consistently maximized some objective -a mathematical representation of the goal an individual seeks to achieve through their choices.
Reasoning that more of a good thing was always better than less, he concluded that the only rational objective was to maximize long-term average outcomes or returns.
Humans, he argued, should simply be behaving consistently to get more of what they liked and less of what they disliked.

That strategy, now called expected value theory, was used to define rational decision-making in domains ranging from religious beliefs (Pascal, 1670), to fear of accidental death, to wealth maximization (Arnauld & Nicole, 1996).
text.formatted: That strategy, now called expected value theory, was used to define rational decision-making in domains ranging from religious beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pascal, 1670)</ref>, to fear of accidental death, to wealth maximization <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arnauld & Nicole, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, Pascal's hypothesis rested on two key insights: First, that the objective value of an option is simply the product of gain (or loss) and the probability of that outcome (Pascal & Fermat, 1654).
text.formatted: Overall, Pascal's hypothesis rested on two key insights: First, that the objective value of an option is simply the product of gain (or loss) and the probability of that outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Pascal & Fermat, 1654)</ref>.

text.text: Second, that humans should rationally structure their choices to consistently pursue their goals (Pascal, 1670).
text.formatted: Second, that humans should rationally structure their choices to consistently pursue their goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pascal, 1670)</ref>.

text.text: Since Pascal, choice theory has, perhaps unfortunately, undergone a series of revolutions that have shifted it away from this relatively simple and intuitive framework.

The first shift was driven by the observation that humans often exhibit what is called risk-averse behavior, apparently preferring lower long-run earnings in order to minimize variance across their possible outcomes.
Daniel Bernoulli recognized that this riskaversion was incompatible with most scholars' understanding of Pascal's ideas.

He argued that humans act to maximize a different objective, the mathematical product of a logarithmic transformation of gain (the utility function) and the probability of receiving that gain (Bernoulli, 1738).
text.formatted: He argued that humans act to maximize a different objective, the mathematical product of a logarithmic transformation of gain (the utility function) and the probability of receiving that gain <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bernoulli, 1738)</ref>.

text.text: By the mid-20th century, the notion of what humans were trying to maximize had been relaxed even further based on new mathematical (Pareto, 1906) and theoretical-empirical (Samuelson, 1947) insights.
text.formatted: By the mid-20th century, the notion of what humans were trying to maximize had been relaxed even further based on new mathematical <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Pareto, 1906)</ref> and theoretical-empirical <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Samuelson, 1947)</ref> insights.

text.text: In the expected utility theory, which emerged from these insights, the focus shifted away from the specification of a particular utility function to basic tests of whether observed choice behavior could be accounted for by any utility function at all (Samuelson, 1952; Savage, 1954; Von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944).
text.formatted: In the expected utility theory, which emerged from these insights, the focus shifted away from the specification of a particular utility function to basic tests of whether observed choice behavior could be accounted for by any utility function at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Samuelson, 1952;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Savage, 1954;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944)</ref>.

text.text: Scholars stopped defining what a given individual should maximize, they simply tested whether observed behavior was consistently aimed at maximizing any goal at all.
By the 1970s, however, it was clear that human choices were not reliably pursuing even the most byzantine of fixed utility functions (Allais, 1953; Ellsberg, 1961).
text.formatted: By the 1970s, however, it was clear that human choices were not reliably pursuing even the most byzantine of fixed utility functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allais, 1953;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Ellsberg, 1961)</ref>.

text.text: These observations led many economists and psychologists to abandon the notion that behavior was logically consistent: that behavior reflected the rational pursuit of any goal at all.
Accordingly, psychologists shifted away from making statements about why humans made the choices they did, or even from making statements about what humans should choose.

Instead, they shifted towards simply predicting what a given human chooser would do in a given situation. Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981), in their seminal work defining prospect theory, laid the foundation for these purely predictive theories, abandoning logical consistency (or more formally: transitivity) in favor of descriptive power.
text.formatted: Instead, they shifted towards simply predicting what a given human chooser would do in a given situation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Tversky & Kahneman, 1981)</ref>, in their seminal work defining prospect theory, laid the foundation for these purely predictive theories, abandoning logical consistency (or more formally: transitivity) in favor of descriptive power.

text.text: Their model adopted a referencedependent representation of utility (formally a value function) with multiple empirically derived features and a subjective notion of probability -all of which varied significantly from individual-to-individual and context-to-context.
With these components, prospect theory and its progeny did a better job of predicting what humans do choose.
What the theory lacked, however, was an explanation of why people made such apparently inconsistent and undirected decisions.
Here, we employ a new approach in an effort to explain the why of many of the classes of choice behavior that Kahneman and Tversky accurately described.
To accomplish this goal, we first return to the simplest possible objective: Pascal's assertion that people want to go home with as much good-stuff as possiblefoot_0 .
text.formatted: To accomplish this goal, we first return to the simplest possible objective: Pascal's assertion that people want to go home with as much good-stuff as possible<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> .

text.text: In the spirit of Herb Simon (Simon, 1955), we acknowledge that humans have limited cognitive capacity, and that adding capacity always comes at a cost (a requirement we have shown is imposed by the laws of physics (Steverson et al., 2019)).
text.formatted: In the spirit of Herb Simon <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Simon, 1955)</ref>, we acknowledge that humans have limited cognitive capacity, and that adding capacity always comes at a cost (a requirement we have shown is imposed by the laws of physics <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Steverson et al., 2019)</ref>).

text.text: We define cognitive capacity in the domain of human decision-making as a limit on representational precision (the entropy of the representation), capturing the notion that a given finite level of precision acts as a kind of filter which conditions our internal representation.
How does a simple expected value-like objective combine with limited precision to define optimal choice behavior?
We argue that the human nervous system must, in essence, balance the costs of precision against the gains achieved by a more accurate maximization of expected value (Steverson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: We argue that the human nervous system must, in essence, balance the costs of precision against the gains achieved by a more accurate maximization of expected value <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Steverson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Drawing inspiration from Bayesian Theory (Bayes, 1763) and Signal Detection Theory (Green & Swets, 2000), we acknowledge that computing the tradeoff between cost and benefit when the world is imprecisely represented requires some knowledge about the structure of the choice environment (essentially a distributional Bayesian prior).
text.formatted: Drawing inspiration from Bayesian Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bayes, 1763)</ref> and Signal Detection Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Green & Swets, 2000)</ref>, we acknowledge that computing the tradeoff between cost and benefit when the world is imprecisely represented requires some knowledge about the structure of the choice environment (essentially a distributional Bayesian prior).

text.text: We conclude that if the chooser takes as inputs a knowledge (perhaps imperfect) of the structure of the choice environment and knowledge of their own level of precision, they can use that information to select an optimal task-appropriate utility function.

This kind of utility function, one selected implicitly by the brain, can be conceptualized as a tool selected by the decision-maker to sculpt their internal representation of value in a way that maximizes average earnings (or minimizes errors) given the limits of their precision.
In our construction, the objective-of-choice (maximizing reward or minimizing errors) and the utility function are thus formally separated.
The utility function (and the risk attitude it implies) becomes a tool used by the nervous system to achieve the simplest possible goal.

Once we employ this approach, we find that many features of human choice previously thought of as irrational resolve as simple strategies for consistent maximization given the constraints imposed by physics on the human brain.
Our approach thus differs from many classical approaches in a number of ways: • We assume that the detailed probabilistic structure of the current reward environment matters to choosers.

This represents a significant departure from most mainstream theories in economics and psychology that define a choice problem as the (sometimes probabilistic) options faced by a decision-maker but leave out the likelihood with which each option is encountered.
We consider the likelihood that any given option becomes available for choice to be fundamental for the meaningful specification of a choice problem.
In this, we deviate from classical and neoclassical economics, requiring a different and more complete specification of the choice environment as a fundamental part of the choice problem.

• Following Pascal, we assume that a decision-maker's goal is either to 1) maximize long-run average earnings, or 2) minimize their error rates (where an error is choosing an option other than the one that maximizes earnings).
Thus, we abandon the notion that humans want to minimize risk in the situations we are modeling.
Risk attitudes emerge, in our approach, as a byproduct of the utility functions that choosers select to maximize their objective goals.
• Like most previous theorists, we assume that humans transform objective value inputs to subjective values using a utility-like function.
Where we differ from traditional approaches is that we place that representational function under the (non-conscious) control of the chooser (either by their brain or by evolution).
In the language of economics, we endogenize the utility function and separate it from their objective.

• We initially leave as a free parameter the precise level of cognitive capacity available to the chooser, examining exhaustively the optimal utility functions that emerge for choosers at any possible level of precision.
In our approach, different levels of cognitive capacity are a primary source of individual variation.
(A secondary source of variation arises from the subject's individually held prior about the reward distribution of the environment.)

Perhaps surprisingly, we find that once the utility function is under the control of the chooser, the advantage incurred by increasing cognitive capacity (which we define formally below) is often surprisingly small.
Losses produced by having low cognitive capacity can often be well-compensated for with simple changes to the utility function.
In the language of economics: the returns-to-precision are less than might be expected.

• In an allied paper (Glimcher et al., 2026), we extend this set of observations and explore the notion that allocated cognitive capacity itself may also be under the control of the chooser (at least to some extent).
text.formatted: • In an allied paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Glimcher et al., 2026)</ref>, we extend this set of observations and explore the notion that allocated cognitive capacity itself may also be under the control of the chooser (at least to some extent).

text.text: In that extension of this work, we define the precise cost of precision and allow the chooser to optimally select how much precision to purchase before selecting a utility function.
This final phase of our approach allows us to fully define human choice as an optimization problem where the only currently unmeasured parameter is the cost of precision to the decision-maker.

One unique feature of this approach is that it defines the entire choice problem and specifies the utility function and the chooser's stochasticity without resorting to any free parameters in the model of theory.
This approach is, in essence, a one parameter model of decision-making that can account for all of behaviors observed in prospect theory.
The work presented here, it should be noted, stops short of exploring decisions over risky lotteries.
While in this paper, we view the world as probabilistic, we explore choices which arise in that probabilistic world that are always made between two certain outcomes.
In the discussion section, we describe how our approach can be extended to the domain of risky choice.

We wish to be explicit about this scope restriction: the theoretical framework, analytical derivations, and simulations presented in this paper apply exclusively to this class of riskless choice -although we find that many classes of puzzling behavior classically associated with risky-choice may not involve risk at all.
We adopt this restriction deliberately to isolate the role of representational capacity in shaping value functions, without introducing the additional complexity of probability representation.
Readers seeking a general theory of decision under risk will find that our current results, while suggestive, do not yet constitute one.
Our approach, however, is extensible to the domain of risky choice and a second presentation of that set of extensions is forthcoming.
What stands out for us in this theory of decision-making amongst certain outcomes is how many puzzling phenomena become easily explainable.

The sigmoidal value function of Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), the concave utility function of Bernoulli (Bernoulli, 1738), and the linear utility function of Pascal (Pascal, 1670) all emerge as nested examples of rational strategies that are required of choosers who face different environments with varying degrees of precision.
text.formatted: The sigmoidal value function of <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)</ref>, the concave utility function of Bernoulli <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bernoulli, 1738)</ref>, and the linear utility function of Pascal <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pascal, 1670)</ref> all emerge as nested examples of rational strategies that are required of choosers who face different environments with varying degrees of precision.

text.text: It is in this regard that we hope our approach has the most impact, effectively serving as a theory of why seemingly irrational behaviors and distortions from objective value-coding emerge.
We note that our approach is closely related to a number of recent approaches that have inspired and shaped this work.

Of particular note, our work descends from the original theory of stochastic choice pioneered by McFadden (McFadden, 1973), whose random utility framework models the probabilistic nature of observed choices by adding noise to an otherwise fixed utility function.
text.formatted: Of particular note, our work descends from the original theory of stochastic choice pioneered by <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">McFadden (McFadden, 1973)</ref>, whose random utility framework models the probabilistic nature of observed choices by adding noise to an otherwise fixed utility function.

text.text: The key difference between our framework and that of McFadden is that in his specification, the utility function and the noise distribution are both exogenous and separately specified, whereas in ours, the utility function is selected by the chooser in response to their noise level.
However, like McFadden, we rely principally on an additive Gaussian noise term, although this is not required.
In the Supplementary Materials we show that our findings are robust to other noise specifications, including those explored by Zhou et al., (2024) for efficient sensory encoding.
text.formatted: In the Supplementary Materials we show that our findings are robust to other noise specifications, including those explored by <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Zhou et al., (2024)</ref> for efficient sensory encoding.

text.text: In an extension of this work (Glimcher et al., 2026), we show that even the noise level, irrespective of the distributional structure of the noise, can be selected by the chooser in response to a specified cost-of-cognition -further reducing the number of free parameters required for this approach.
text.formatted: In an extension of this work <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Glimcher et al., 2026)</ref>, we show that even the noise level, irrespective of the distributional structure of the noise, can be selected by the chooser in response to a specified cost-of-cognition -further reducing the number of free parameters required for this approach.

text.text: We focus on the two objectives of expected earnings maximization and error minimization as these represent the two most theoretically grounded and empirically motivated candidates in the literature, descending respectively from Pascal's normative benchmark and from the empirical works (Robson, 2001; Polanía et al., 2019; Woodford, 2014).
text.formatted: We focus on the two objectives of expected earnings maximization and error minimization as these represent the two most theoretically grounded and empirically motivated candidates in the literature, descending respectively from Pascal's normative benchmark and from the empirical works <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Robson, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Polanía et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Woodford, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: With regard to other closely related work, we note that our approach descends from efficient-coding and noisy-representation accounts of value and choice, which show that distortions in value or probability can arise as optimal adaptations to limited precision (Glimcher, 2011).
text.formatted: With regard to other closely related work, we note that our approach descends from efficient-coding and noisy-representation accounts of value and choice, which show that distortions in value or probability can arise as optimal adaptations to limited precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Glimcher, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In one prominent example derived from Glimcher (2011), Woodford (2014) derived stochastic choice behavior from Shannon capacity constraints under rational inattention. Polanía, Woodford & Ruff (2019) extended this approach by providing neural and behavioral evidence that the brain adapts its representational resolution to the prior distribution of experienced outcomes. Khaw, Li, & Woodford (2021) demonstrated that log-normally distributed noise in value representations produces apparent small-stakes risk aversion. Barretto-García et al. (2023) extended this to individual differences in risk attitudes. Frydman & Jin (2021) derived both utility curvature and probability weighting from efficient coding of risky lotteries. Juechems et al. (2021) derived optimal utility and probability functions for agents with finite computational precision. Heng, Woodford & Polanía (2020) showed that humans adapt their sampling behavior to environmental distributions to economize on cognitive resources.
text.formatted: In one prominent example derived from <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glimcher (2011)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Woodford (2014)</ref> derived stochastic choice behavior from Shannon capacity constraints under rational inattention. <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Polanía, Woodford & Ruff (2019)</ref> extended this approach by providing neural and behavioral evidence that the brain adapts its representational resolution to the prior distribution of experienced outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Khaw, Li, & Woodford (2021)</ref> demonstrated that log-normally distributed noise in value representations produces apparent small-stakes risk aversion. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Barretto-García et al. (2023)</ref> extended this to individual differences in risk attitudes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Frydman & Jin (2021)</ref> derived both utility curvature and probability weighting from efficient coding of risky lotteries. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Juechems et al. (2021)</ref> derived optimal utility and probability functions for agents with finite computational precision. <ref type="bibr">Heng, Woodford & Polanía (2020)</ref> showed that humans adapt their sampling behavior to environmental distributions to economize on cognitive resources.

text.text: We share with all of these papers, which descend from Glimcher (2011), the central premise that apparent distortions in value representation reflect rational adaptation to finite capacity, but innovate and consolidate to yield a single and highly tractable framework.
text.formatted: We share with all of these papers, which descend from <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glimcher (2011)</ref>, the central premise that apparent distortions in value representation reflect rational adaptation to finite capacity, but innovate and consolidate to yield a single and highly tractable framework.

text.text: First, we focus on riskless choice between certain outcomes before using our consolidated approach with regard to risky lotteries.

This is not a trivial distinction and extending our framework to risky lotteries requires separately modelling the capacity-constrained representation of outcome probability using exactly the approach proposed here for utility.

Second, and more fundamentally, these accounts derive the utility function as a fixed consequence of a specific coding problem, with a given prior and a given noise model as the universal inputs that drive our model.
Our framework differs fundamentally from these earlier approaches in that for us, the utility function is the explicit variable over which the chooser optimizes.

Third, rather than characterizing a single optimal function for a given prior and noise model, as in these other approaches, we exhaustively map optimal utility functions across the full space of precision levels, from near-zero to near-infinite precision, and across many reward distributions.

This allows us to generate the full family of optimal functions as a continuous output and allows our approach to be used in almost any situation, rather than yielding a point solution for a particular problem of interest.

We also find, for the first time, that the returns to increasing cognitive precision are surprisingly small once the utility function is optimally adjusted to the available capacity, with a doubling of encoding resources yielding only a two to three percent improvement in average earnings.
Our approach also incorporates important features of the Decision-by-Sampling literature (e.g., Stewart et al., 2006 Stewart et al., , 2015)).
text.formatted: Our approach also incorporates important features of the Decision-by-Sampling literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Stewart et al., 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stewart et al., , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: In that literature, Bhui & Gershman (2018) provided an important normative foundation for our general approach, showing that rank-based sampling is formally equivalent to efficient coding.
text.formatted: In that literature, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bhui & Gershman (2018)</ref> provided an important normative foundation for our general approach, showing that rank-based sampling is formally equivalent to efficient coding.

text.text: Our framework also, of course, captures ideas from evolutionary and biological accounts of utility (Netzer, 2009; Netzer et al., 2025; Rayo & Becker, 2007; Robson, 2001; Robson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Our framework also, of course, captures ideas from evolutionary and biological accounts of utility <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Netzer, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Netzer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Rayo & Becker, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Robson, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Robson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: What unifies all these accounts, and what we adopt from them, is the principle that the utility function is an optimized response to the structure of the environment and the constraints under which choices are made.

Our approach departs from these in that we treat the full probabilistic structure of the reward environment as a formal component of the choice problem and treat the function as both dynamic and fully endogenous to the chooser.

Finally, our work is also closely related to, and draws deep inspiration from, recent contributions that study the cognitive limits of valuation and choice, including work by Charness et al. (2013), Oprea (2024), and Webb et al. (2021).
text.formatted: Finally, our work is also closely related to, and draws deep inspiration from, recent contributions that study the cognitive limits of valuation and choice, including work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Charness et al. (2013)</ref>, Oprea (2024), and <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Webb et al. (2021)</ref>.

text.text: These papers collectively establish that there is substantial individual variation in the quality of utility maximization that cannot be captured by a single fixed utility function, and that cognitive limits are a primary driver of that variation.

Our approach complements this literature by providing a normative account of how valuation itself should adapt to such constraints, rather than treating the resulting utility distortions as exogenous or descriptive.
We present our methods in two ways.
In sections 2.1-2.3, we present a formal mathematical specification of the problem we set out to solve, which may not be appropriate for all readers.
In section 2.4, we present a graphical overview of our methods that should be appropriate for all readers.
Readers with a deep mathematical interest in our approach should read all four sections.
Readers with intermediate interest are encouraged to skip sections 2.2 and 2.3.
Readers interested in the general approach should proceed directly to section 2.4.

It is also important to note that in attempting to answer the larger question: What is the optimal utility function for a given environment when facing a riskless choice problem, we have developed three overlapping mathematical approaches.

We have developed a proof-based approach, an analytic approach that relies on features of Gaussian noise to achieve computational simplicity, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo-based approach which can solve essentially any choice problem.
The latter two approaches are described in this paper.
Interested readers can examine the proof-based approach in an adjacent economicsstyle paper, which is partially overlapping in content but aimed at an economics audience (Glimcher et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Interested readers can examine the proof-based approach in an adjacent economicsstyle paper, which is partially overlapping in content but aimed at an economics audience <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Glimcher et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The analytic approach generalizes that purely mathematical solution to environments in which choosers face a larger number of possible reward values 2 .
The bulk of the material presented here relies on this analytic approach.

This analytic approach, however, cannot be used to identify an optimal utility function when the decision-maker must choose between more than two options (a change which has a significant impact on the shape of the optimal utility function).
For that class of problems, we generalize our solution to a numerical Monte-Carlo-style strategy (Metropolis & Ulam, 1949).
text.formatted: For that class of problems, we generalize our solution to a numerical Monte-Carlo-style strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Metropolis & Ulam, 1949)</ref>.

text.text: This allows us to solve for optimal utility functions under essentially any conditions.
We begin by stating explicitly the objective of the chooser is either to 1) maximize average earnings or 2) minimize the number of errors.
Our goal is to recover an optimal utility function 𝑢(𝑥), which is dependent on the choice environment 3 and the cognitive capacity of the chooser, and which maximizes the stated objective function.

The choice environment is defined by a formal set containing a fixed number, 𝑚, of possible rewards (or punishments) which we call 𝑋 = {𝑥 ! , . . . , 𝑥 " }, where each 𝑥 # is a real number (a possible reward value that the decision-maker can encounter).
Without loss of generality, but to make the problem more intuitive for this presentation, we assume that 𝑥 !
≤ 𝑥 $ ≤. .. ≤ 𝑥 " (thus 𝑥 " is always used to label the largest possible reward and 𝑥 !
the smallest).
Additionally, we assume that each next reward in 𝑋 increases in objective value by the same increment, for example, by one dollar.
Choice sets are constructed by drawing one or more possible rewards from the set 𝑋.
A decision-maker's task is to select one option from a given choice set.
The probability that any given reward will be drawn from the environment (𝑋) into a choice set with 𝑛 possible rewards is specified by a probability distribution 4.

text.text: We adopt weak rather than strict monotonicity to allow for the possibility that a decision-maker is indifferent between two reward levels, that is, that two objectively different rewards may be assigned the same subjective utility.
We also assume that the utility function u is bounded between 0 and 1 (i.e.0 ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 !
) ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 $ ) ≤. .. ≤ 𝑢(𝑥 " ) ≤ 1), such that there is a maximum possible level of utility a person can experience.

Restricting the utility function so that it cannot have an infinite range goes against a feature of many standard economic models (e.g., Bernoulli, 1738) but anchors our theory to the physical world the human nervous system occupies and is a fundamental constraint on our theory.
Together, these two assumptions define the candidate set of utility functions considered throughout this paper.
No further parametric restrictions are imposed, and we do not assume any functional form, such as power utility or logarithmic utility.

The optimal utility function 𝑢 * is identified by searching exhaustively over this entire candidate set, making our approach, uniquely, nonparametric with respect to the shape of the utility function.
Note that we adopt the convention that a capital 𝑈 calls out the noise-contaminated form of noisy utility while u calls out the noiseless, or mean, utility function.

Our approach can be generalized to other patterns of noise (such as Weber-style multiplicative noise terms), but we begin with this simpler specification which can be tied to our formal proof that requires an additive noise term (Glimcher et al., 2026).

To standardize this representation and allow more direct comparison across choosers with different levels of precision, we express utility in units of representational noise.
In the additive Gaussian noise model, where noise is fixed across the utility range, this amounts to rescaling the bounded utility function by its standard deviation.
We apply a transformation to the utility by redefining the units of utility as capacity with an upper bound of 𝑢(𝑥) at 𝑐 (the maximum capacity of a given chooser) as:
After this rescaling, the range of the y-axis (from 0 to 𝑐) captures the capacity of the chooser, measured in the number of standard deviations which that chooser can employ for reward encoding.

In this representation, high-capacity (low-noise) choosers have utility functions that span more standard deviations and low-capacity choosers have utility functions that span fewer standard deviations.

This transformation has the benefit of effectively recasting the utility space into a natural unit of standard deviations, allowing direct comparison between choosers of different precision (a transformation first suggested by McFadden, (1973)).

text.text: More generally, we use the term capacity to refer to the effective signal-to-noise structure of the internal representation, the extent to which differences in the utility of two or more options can be reliably distinguished given the noise embedded in the representation.
The precise mathematical definition of capacity is therefore model-dependent.

In the Gaussian case considered in this section, it is naturally expressed as the inverse of a fixed noise parameter, whereas under the alternative noise structure presented in the Supplementary Materials (Poisson-like variability), capacity corresponds more closely to the overall scaling of the utility function.

For simplicity and because the analytical results that follow here have an additive Gaussian noise structure, in the remainder of the paper, we represent all choosers with regard to their maximum capacity in units of standard deviation, 𝜎, which we take to be the natural units of utility under this specification.
In this section, we present our analytical mathematical approach to derive the optimal utility function.
(A graphical presentation of this approach can be found below in section 2.4 which may be of greater interest for many readers who might choose to skip ahead to that section.)
This approach requires the following simplifications, two of which can be relaxed in the next section: 1) That the utility axis is discrete rather than continuous.
2) That choosers must select from only two options on a given trial.
3) That the choice options be drawn i.i.d. from the environment.
For this first example, we choose an environment in which rewards can take a maximum of four discrete values.
Any efficient decision-maker will necessarily make use of the whole range of utilities that are available to them.

Knowing how to recover the probability of an error for any specific choice between two options for any utility function at any given capacity, we can proceed to calculate the overall earnings (gains or losses) and error rates associated with any particular utility function in any given environment.
We accomplish this in two stages.
First, for each choice set under a given utility function, we calculate the probability of an error as well as expected earnings.
Then, after we calculate this for all possible choice pairs, we total up the aggregate errors and earnings while taking into account how often each choice set is encountered in the given environment.
Below, we formally describe this process for our two optimality criteria: (1) maximizing earnings and (2) minimizing the number of errors.
We start by determining the expected earnings that any given utility function delivers for a chooser with a given capacity.

This separation between the currency of decision-making and the currency of evaluation is fundamental to our framework.
The utility function determines how the decision is made, but the quality of that decision is evaluated by what is received, a quantity the chooser is actually trying to maximize.

An alternative approach is to define optimal utility as the utility function that minimized the number of errors made by the decision-maker, regardless of the earnings loss associated with those errors.
Under this criterion, the optimal utility function 𝑢 * is the one that leads to the fewest incorrect choices across all choice sets.
These two approaches are importantly distinct.
When maximizing rewards, making an error when choosing between an objective value of 1 and an objective value of 4 is much worse than making an error when choosing between values of 3 and 4.
When minimizing errors, these two erroneous choices have equal impact on the optimization problem.

The analytic approach described above can be used to identify optimal utility functions when the choice sets (the options being compared) contain only two options with rewards independently drawn from the environment (where the environment is defined by the set X and its attendant probabilities of occurrence).

The key limitation of this approach is that the exact probability of correctly identifying the best option relies on the closed-form properties of the difference of two independent Gaussian random variables (a difference which is described by a Gaussian).

When decision-makers must choose between more than two options or choice sets have complex covariance structures that make the rewards non-independent, this specific closed-form expression is no longer available, and the error probability cannot be derived analytically in the same tractable way.
For those choice conditions, we use a Monte-Carlo-style simulation to identify the optimal utility function.
As with our analytic solution, we begin by specifying the choice environment and the capacity of the chooser (the level of internal noise).
As before, the utilities for the lowest reward value and the highest reward value are set to 0 and 𝑐, respectively.
As before, we generate a list of all utility functions we wish to consider: {𝑢 ! , 𝑢 $ , . . . , 𝑢 ) }.

Next, for each 𝑢, we simulate one million choices and calculate either the earnings (for the reward maximization objective) or the number of errors (for the number of error minimization objective) across these simulated choices.
Our procedure is as follows: We assume a candidate utility, 𝑢 # , and a capacity level, 𝑐.
Next, we draw one million choice sets (choice problems) according to the environmental reward probability structure.
Then, one choice set at a time, we assign a noisy utility to each reward in this choice set following 𝑈(𝑥 # ) = 𝑢(𝑥 # ) + 𝜀 # .
Then, the algorithm selects from this choice set the reward with the highest noisy utility 𝑈.
After doing this for one million choice sets, we compute the average earnings and the total number of errors for the assumed 𝑢 # with capacity level 𝑐.
Finally, to identify the optimal utility function, we select the one that maximizes expected reward or minimizes the total error.

In the preceding sections, we restricted our analysis to binary choice sets -choices between two options.
To generalize the framework, we extend our investigation to larger choice sets; situations in which a decision maker must choose amongst three or more options.
This class of optimization problem is too complex to solve using the analytical method used in the preceding section.
We therefore use a Monte-Carlo simulation.

By simulating millions of choices drawn randomly according to the stated probability distribution for the environment, we can obtain approximations of optimal utility structures under these more complex conditions.
(To validate this methodology, we show that it replicates the results obtained from the analytical example above in the Supplementary Materials.)

text.text: Note that despite the chooser's consistent objective, to maximize total earnings, the resulting optimal utility functions, 𝑢 * , exhibit systematic variations across choice environments: • In the case of a positively skewed environment, 𝑢 * is concave, consistent with Bernoulli-like riskaversion.
When low-valued rewards are most common, limited capacity choosers maximize their average rate-of-return by adopting utility functions that would be classically described as riskaverse.
They do this because they are attempting to maximize their ability to discriminate between the more commonly available low-value options.

We note that the original utility function proposed by Bernoulli (Bernoulli, 1738) took essentially this form and the choice problem he was trying to explain (the St Petersburg Paradox) had a positively skewed distribution of possible rewards, just as this example.
text.formatted: We note that the original utility function proposed by Bernoulli <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bernoulli, 1738)</ref> took essentially this form and the choice problem he was trying to explain (the St Petersburg Paradox) had a positively skewed distribution of possible rewards, just as this example.

text.text: This may suggest that Bernoulli's utility function would be optimal for a chooser trying to maximize reward in the St Petersburg game environment, with the caveat that the classic game explicitly involves risk which is not directly modeled here.

• When all options are equally probable, in a uniformly distributed environment, 𝑢 * is sigmoidal, suggesting an adaptive balance between what might be classically described as risk-aversion and risk-seeking behavior.
The function exhibits greater sensitivity to mid-range values, ensuring efficient differentiation across the entire value spectrum which minimizes the most-costly mistakes, erroneously selecting 𝑥 !
or 𝑥 $ when 𝑥 ; is available.

We note that the original sigmoidal utility function of Kahneman and Tversky was largely developed to account for behavioral data from experiments in which the probabilities of encountering a given reward were uniformly distributed.

The prospect theory utility function developed for risky choice, although quite different from Bernoulli's function, might be seen as an optimal strategy for maximizing reward, this time in an experimental psychology laboratory.
• In a negatively skewed environment, 𝑢 * is convex, which would imply risk-seeking behavior where lotteries are employed, a strategy that prioritizes differentiation among common high-value options.
Thus, a convex utility can, under some conditions, be optimal.

This stands in stark contrast to the standard economic conclusion that such functions, at least in the domain of risky-choice, are considered irrational because they violate second-order stochastic dominance.

text.text: For low capacities: In a positively skewed environment, 𝑢 * exhibits a starkly concave shape.
This would be classically viewed as implying risk aversion and a strategy that prioritizes differentiation among lowervalue options.
In a uniformly distributed choice environment 𝑢 * follows the classical S-shaped form, indicating sensitivity to mid-range values.
In a negatively skewed environment 𝑢 * takes a convex shape, improving discrimination amongst common highly valued rewards.
As capacity increases, however, 𝑢 * in each environment progressively approaches a linear form.

This transition suggests that with higher levels of capacity, when the system can encode reward values more precisely, the need for nonlinear transformations that prioritize differentiation among specific ranges is reduced.
The right-most panels show the average rates-of-return for each of these cognitive capacity levels, in each of these environments.
We plot them as a percent improvement over the rate-of-return achieved by a fully random chooser (one with zero cognitive capacity).
What stands out from these data is that a two standard deviation chooser does much better than a random chooser.
Adding a third standard deviation of capacity yields significant but diminishing returns.
The 'returns-for-capacity,' however, decline quite quickly.
Consider a chooser with 4 standard deviations of noise versus a chooser with 8 standard deviations of noise.
Neurobiologically, this might be thought of as equivalent to doubling the number of neurons encoding the utility function.
In this case, a doubling of the number of neurons (or alternatively, perhaps doubling the number of possible action potentials) yields only a 2-3% increase in overall gains.

For a decision-maker who can set their own utility function, it might not make much sense to spend a lot of metabolic energy creating additional cognitive capacity if it achieves very little additional gain.

text.text: With an expanded set of possible rewards, we observe the consistent emergence of an S-shaped 𝑢 * as the optimal function across all choice environments, when capacity is low.
This pattern is not limited to the uniform distribution but can also be seen in positively and negatively skewed environments for very low-capacity choosers.
As capacity increases in a positively skewed environment, 𝑢 * transitions from an S-shaped form to a concave function and eventually approaches a linear form as capacity grows.
In a uniformly distributed environment, the S-shaped function is stable until relatively high capacities, those at which the optimal function becomes linear.
In a negatively skewed environment, increasing capacity shifts 𝑢 * from an Sshaped curve to a convex form before ultimately converging to a linear function.
This highlights the fact that for reasonably large ranges of possible rewards, very low-capacity choosers universally show the Sshaped utility function as optimal.

As capacity increases above this very low level, we see the expected pattern of risk-aversion-like curvature in right-skewed environments and the expected pattern of riskseeking-like curvature in left-skewed environments.
Figure 11 plots these same analyses, but here for a chooser minimizing their expected error rate.
These functions remain largely similar, but it should be noted that they transition slightly more rapidly to the linear shape than in the reward maximization setting.
These variations suggest that while increased capacity aligns decision-making strategies across both frameworks, constraints on capacity drive distinct adaptations in the encoding of value.

The results from sections 3.2 and 3.3 make it clear that, for the three environments we have examined, it is very difficult to use the shape of the utility function to infer whether the decision-maker is optimizing for average reward or minimizing error.
There would be great value in identifying an environment in which the two objective functions are distinct.
Woodford and colleagues (Polanía et al., 2019; Woodford, 2014) have conducted experiments that suggest human decision-makers may be seeking to minimize errors.

text.text: To enhance the strength of those conclusions, it might be of value to identify an environment in which these two objective functions are more distinct.
Here, we show that bimodally distributed environments have this property.

A limit of the analytic approach employed up to this point is that it cannot identify optimal utility functions when there are more than two alternatives in the choice set.

Here, we show that a strategy of exhaustive simulation, which does not have this limitation, can be used to identify optimal utility functions under essentially any conditions (details in the Methods section).

We first validated our Monte Carlo solution by confirming that it replicates the results of the analytic method for binary choice problems across all three canonical environments; this validation is presented in Supplementary Materials Section B. The third row of the figure shows how these optimal utility functions change when four options are drawn at random from the choice environment and the decision-maker must select a single option from this four-option set.
The fourth and fifth rows present functions for choice set sizes of 6 and 10.
Notice that as the choice set size grows, the functions noticeably steepen to the right.
This is a key insight that has not yet been the subject of much inquiry by economists or psychologists.
The goal of the utility function that maximizes the average rate of return is to discriminate effectively amongst the highest valued of the available options.
As the number of options in the choice set grows, the likelihood that at least one option will be very highly valued also grows.
This puts a premium on making an effective discrimination amongst the most highly valued options, causing the functions to steepen to the right as the size of the choice set grows.
The novel implication of this finding is that for an optimal chooser, risk attitudes should depend on choice set size.
>Empirical Evaluation
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Empirical Evaluation</head>

text.text: To provide an initial empirical assessment of our framework and to define the procedures required for fitting empirical data to our theory, we reanalyzed data from a previously collected two-stage experiment (Kurtz-David et al., 2024).
text.formatted: To provide an initial empirical assessment of our framework and to define the procedures required for fitting empirical data to our theory, we reanalyzed data from a previously collected two-stage experiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kurtz-David et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: That experiment was designed to examine how value representations adapt when the statistical structure of the choice environment is changed, a core feature of our theory.

In Stage 1 of that existing experiment, a stage used to preselect homogeneous and reliable choosers, participants reported their willingness to pay for each of 33 50-50 lotteries using a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) method, with one randomly selected trial implemented for payment.
These valuations were used to estimate an individual subjective-value function using a power-utility specification.

For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1).
text.formatted: For subjects proceeding to Stage 2, participants were selected whose risk aversion during the BDM bidding procedure (which is known to be distinct from their risk aversion level during choice) was narrowly bounded (𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑣𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑒 𝑎𝑡 0.9 < 𝜌 < 1.1).

text.text: In Stage 2, on two separate days, subjects made binary choices between 50-50 binary lotteries with two different monetary outcomes each of which ranged from $0 to $60, with 320 decision problems presented on each day.

Only the distribution of lottery values differed across the days: values were drawn either from a Uniform distribution or from a Pareto Type III distribution, with the order of the two environments counterbalanced across participants.

Because each participant experienced both environments, the dataset allows us to examine how estimates of representational capacity (and the shape of the optimal utility function) change within the same individual as the environmental statistics change.

This permits us to examine two properties of the capacity estimates obtained from our framework: 1) whether individual differences in estimated capacity are preserved across environments, consistent with capacity reflecting a relatively stable individual constraint on reward representation; and 2) whether the level of estimated capacity also changes with the statistical structure of the environment, potentially reflecting differences in the benefits of allocating cognitive resources.
Recall that our theory was specifically designed to predict precisely when and how errors (failures to pick the higher valued option) occur, this differs from most standard models.
We also treat the objective value axis as discrete in our theory, another important difference.
For each participant, we therefore first discretized the range of lottery expected values into subject-specific value bins.

To ensure that the two environments were evaluated on a common value scale, the bin boundaries were defined as evenly spaced quantiles of choice problems using the participant's lottery values in the Uniform environment and then held fixed for the Pareto environment.

The expected values of both options from all Uniform trials were thus pooled and divided into 12 equally populated bins using a simple quantile-based binning procedure with the lower and upper boundaries fixed at the minimum ($0) and maximum ($60) values encountered.
These same 12 bins were then also employed in the Pareto environment.
The midpoint of each bin was used as its representative value.
For each environment, every binary-choice trial was thus assigned to a pair of value bins according to the expected values of its two options 7 .
A choice was classified as an error if the participant selected the option with the lower expected value.
For every choice-pair (or more precisely for every choice-pair bin), we calculated both the number of observed choices involving that pair and the proportion of those choices that were errors.
This yielded a symmetric empirical error matrix for each participant for each environment.
The trials in which both options fell within the same value bin, the diagonal cells, were excluded from model fitting as errors are not possible in those bins.
To avoid fitting to error rates determined by a single observation, cells containing fewer than two trials were also excluded from our analysis.
Only one triangular half of the symmetric matrix is presented, which captures all possible pairwise choices.
An example of such a matrix for a subject can be seen in Figure 16D.
text.formatted: An example of such a matrix for a subject can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">16D</ref>.

text.text: Recall that our theory rests on the notion that choosers adapt their utility functions to the current environment in order to maximize overall returns.

In order to most precisely specify the environment each chooser encountered, we used how often each value bin appeared in the participant's choices to describe the specific value environment that chooser experienced.
For each bin (and hence choice problem), we counted how often an error was observed in that bin and how many total problems were encountered by that chooser in that bin.
Dividing errors by the total number of encountered problems we derived an error rate and a total count for each bin.
This gave us the probability of encountering each value bin in that environment and the error rate observed in that bin for that chooser.
Our goal is to derive, for the observed choice environment defined by the encounter rates, optimal utility functions for every possible capacity level.

Once these optimal utility functions have been derived for this specific environment at each possible capacity level, we can convert these optimal utility functions into predicted error rates that should have been observed in each bin if an ideal chooser was employing that optimal utility function, and hence the capacity level associated with that utility function.

Using the binomial likelihood to correct for the number of encounters, we can then ask which theoretical error matrix (each associated with a different capacity) best matches the observed error rates produced by a given subject.

Following our theory we thus computed a monotonic utility function that maximized expected earnings at each capacity level, calculated independently for each environment encountered by each chooser over a grid of capacities from 1 to 20 in steps of 0.5.
Figure 16A shows all these optimal utility functions for one example subject.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">16A</ref> shows all these optimal utility functions for one example subject.

text.text: A capacity of 0 here corresponds to a random chooser.
A few examples of this optimal utility function at selected capacities (𝐶 = 20, 7, 4, 2.5) are shown in Figure 16B.

text.text: The resulting distances between represented values in the optimal utility function were used to determine the probability of making an error in each value bin.
Thus, independently for every subject, a predicted (theoretical) error matrix was generated for each level of capacity, examples of which can be seen in Figure 16C.
text.formatted: Thus, independently for every subject, a predicted (theoretical) error matrix was generated for each level of capacity, examples of which can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">16C</ref>.

text.text: Here, each error matrix corresponds to the optimal utility function in Panel B for the respective value of capacity.
Next, we compared each of the theoretical error matrices with the participant's actual empirical error matrix which can be seen in Figure 16D.
text.formatted: Next, we compared each of the theoretical error matrices with the participant's actual empirical error matrix which can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">16D</ref>.

text.text: Our goal was to ask which theoretical error matrix was most likely to have led to the observed empirical error matrix, thus specifying a best estimate of the capacity allocated by each individual chooser to a given environment.

In a statistical sense our procedure reduces to using the theoretical matrix to specify the weighted coin that the subject should have flipped in each bin, and then using the binomial likelihood to simply ask how likely it is that an observed error matrix derived from any given theoretical matrix -allowing for the number of observations in each bin.
Thus, for a cell (𝑖, 𝑗), 𝑛 #, is the number of trials, 𝑘 #, is the number of observed errors, and 𝑝 #, (𝐶) is the predicted probability of error at a capacity of 𝐶.
We evaluated the prediction using the binomial log-likelihood, which are summed across all the eligible non-diagonal cells as:
The participant's best-fitting capacity is formally defined as the capacity that maximizes this summed loglikelihood.
This procedure is carried out independently for the Uniform and Pareto environments, yielding two capacity estimates for each participant.
Figure 16E shows these summed binomial log-likelihoods of the observed error matrix resulting from a given optimal utility function at each capacity value.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">16E</ref> shows these summed binomial log-likelihoods of the observed error matrix resulting from a given optimal utility function at each capacity value.

text.text: The capacity with the highest log-likelihood value is then selected as the best-fitting capacity value for that environment (𝐶 = 7 in the example).
The examples reveal substantial heterogeneity across subjects in both the frequency and structure of choice errors.
The log-likelihoods identify a distinct best-fitting capacity within each environment.
For example, the participant in the first row makes comparatively more errors as can be seen in the corresponding error matrices.
Their estimated capacity is thus towards the lower end of possible capacities, a capacity of 4 in Uniform and a capacity of 1 in Pareto.
Also, note that their performance is very close to a random chooser in the Pareto environment.
The participant in the fourth row of Figure 17 is a nearly perfect subject who makes almost no errors in the trials and their best estimated capacity is 17.5 in Uniform and 17 in Pareto environment.

text.text: As choice errors decrease, the best-fitting capacity generally increases.

It is important to note that the estimated capacity differs between the Uniform and Pareto conditions, but the relative ordering of these example subjects is preserved, individuals with lower capacity in one environment tend to have lower capacity in the other, whereas higher capacity individuals remain comparatively high across environments.
This relationship is examined formally at the population level in the following section.
At the population level, we first examined whether our model identifies stable individual differences in representational capacity.

If capacity reflects an underlying constraint on reward representation, choosers with relatively high estimated capacity in one environment should also have relatively high capacity in another, despite differences in the statistical structure of the choice environment.
We therefore examined whether the capacity estimates obtained independently in the Uniform and Pareto environments were correlated across participants.
The estimated capacitiesfoot_4 in the Uniform and Pareto environments were, as predicted, correlated across participants with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.792 (𝑝 = 0.0003) (Figure 18A).
text.formatted: The estimated capacities<ref type="foot" target="#foot_4">foot_4</ref> in the Uniform and Pareto environments were, as predicted, correlated across participants with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.792 (𝑝 = 0.0003) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_17">18A</ref>).

text.text: Participants with high estimated capacity (or equivalently, a lower cost per unit of allocated capacity) in one environment also had high capacity in the other.
This suggests that the capacity parameter captures relatively stable individual differences in decision-making precision despite changes in the reward environment.
Interestingly, although relative capacity rankings were largely preserved, participants generally had lower estimated capacities in the Pareto environment than in the Uniform environment.

We next examined the earnings associated with the estimated representations (Figure 18B).
text.formatted: We next examined the earnings associated with the estimated representations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_17">18B</ref>).

text.text: In both environments, participants' actual earnings were close to the maximum earnings predicted by our framework at their estimated capacity.
Relative to the optimal earnings in the Uniform environment, optimal earnings in the Pareto environment were 21.3% lower, while participants' actual earnings were 24.9% lower.
Therefore, the environment associated with lower estimated capacities also offered lower potential earnings.
One possible explanation is that participants adjust cognitive resources allocated to a choice problem according to the benefits of additional precision.
If greater capacity is costly, lower potential returns could reduce the incentive to allocate additional capacity.
Although the present analysis does not directly identify the costs of capacity, the observed pattern is consistent with this interpretation.
A formal model of endogenous capacity allocation is developed in Glimcher et al. (2026).
