text.text: We note that we have also examined a standard expected-utility model using these same data for comparison.

The full model specification, cross-environment parameter analysis, and comparison of the EU curvature (𝛼) and noise (𝛿) parameters with the capacity estimates from our framework are provided in Section C of the Supplementary Materials.
In that section we address the challenges of directly comparing our Bernoulli-error analysis and a traditional fitted parameter model.
In general, we find that our model performs comparably to EU on this particular dataset.
Biologists and engineers think of decision-making as a mechanism directed towards achieving an objective goal.
These approaches descend from Pascal, who defined a decision-maker's objective goal as maximizing how much good-stuff they have in the long-run (Pascal, 1670).
text.formatted: These approaches descend from Pascal, who defined a decision-maker's objective goal as maximizing how much good-stuff they have in the long-run <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pascal, 1670)</ref>.

text.text: The notion that human decisions are guided by purely subjective goals, captured by an idiosyncratic utility function that does not maximize how much stuff you have at the end of the day, entered choice theory in the 1700s.
In developing that approach, Bernoulli (Bernoulli, 1738) was motivated by the observation that humans showed an aversion to risks in the famous St.
text.formatted: In developing that approach, Bernoulli <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bernoulli, 1738)</ref> was motivated by the observation that humans showed an aversion to risks in the famous St.

text.text: Petersburg game.
Bernoulli interpreted this behavior as inconsistent with the goal of maximizing objective average rates of return.
In the years that followed, subjective utility functions became the standard for psychologists as well as for economists.

By the late 1900s, with the work of Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981) and their development of an (intransitive) value function, the notion that human decision-making was subjective, could not be considered optimizing, and could not be construed as driven by any clear objective function had become widely accepted.
text.formatted: By the late 1900s, with the work of Kahneman and Tversky <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kahneman & Tversky, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Tversky & Kahneman, 1981)</ref> and their development of an (intransitive) value function, the notion that human decision-making was subjective, could not be considered optimizing, and could not be construed as driven by any clear objective function had become widely accepted.

text.text: There were, however, elements of this approach that raised persistent challenging questions.

Matthew Rabin (Rabin, 2000), for example, showed that if one uses the curvature of the human utility function measured in the laboratory to predict human behavior when making very large purchases of durable goods, it predicts a level of risk aversion that is never observed.
text.formatted: Matthew Rabin <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Rabin, 2000)</ref>, for example, showed that if one uses the curvature of the human utility function measured in the laboratory to predict human behavior when making very large purchases of durable goods, it predicts a level of risk aversion that is never observed.

text.text: What the Rabin Paradox revealed is that the risk aversion implied by the standard utility function approach derived in the laboratory and those derived from realworld analysis of major purchases are incompatible.
Here, we argue that this comes from a misunderstanding of just why the human utility function arises in nature.

In our work (Glimcher et al., 2026) and other recent work like it (Barretto-García et al., 2023; Oprea, 2024), it is hypothesized that the curvature of the human utility function for small stakes decisions has nothing to do with a desire to avoid risk.
text.formatted: In our work <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Glimcher et al., 2026)</ref> and other recent work like it <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barretto-García et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Oprea, 2024)</ref>, it is hypothesized that the curvature of the human utility function for small stakes decisions has nothing to do with a desire to avoid risk.

text.text: For a decision maker with limited cognitive capacity, a curved utility function (which produces what can be interpreted as an aversion to risk) is required if one's goal is to maximize how much good-stuff one has on average.
This leads us to suggest that, at least for small stakes, the utility function is not a goal, but rather a tool.
It is not an objective in and of itself, but a reward encoding strategy used by the nervous system to achieve a different and well-specified objective function.

We believe that this is our key contribution, and an extension of earlier work that has explored similar themes (Barretto-García et al., 2023; Frydman & Jin, 2021; Glimcher, 2011; Khaw et al., 2021; Netzer, 2009; Netzer et al., 2025; Polanía et al., 2019; Rayo & Becker, 2007; Robson, 2001; Robson et al., 2023; Woodford, 2014).
text.formatted: We believe that this is our key contribution, and an extension of earlier work that has explored similar themes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barretto-García et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Frydman & Jin, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glimcher, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Khaw et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Netzer, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Netzer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Polanía et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Rayo & Becker, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Robson, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Robson et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Woodford, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A separation of the objective and utility functions, and a reinterpretation of the utility function as being an empirical tool dynamically configured by the human (and animal) decisional architecture in service of the objective function -at least for small stakes day-to-day decision-making -is, we believe, a necessary and fundamental reanalysis of the utility function that has been gaining traction in the last fifteen years.
In addition to this primary contribution, we can also draw what we believe to be six significant conclusions about the shape of the optimal utility function.

The first of our observations is that the distribution of possible rewards, the context of the choice, determines the shape of the optimal utility function for choosers with limited cognitive capacity.

For choosers facing a world in which small rewards are prevalent and larger rewards are rare (right-skewed distributions), optimal utility functions are concave and resemble the kinds of risk-averse utility functions Bernoulli favored.

In fact, if we write out the specific distribution of possible rewards in the famous St Petersburg gamefoot_5 , we discover that the optimal utility function is almost exactly the function Bernoulli proposed (𝑙𝑜𝑔 (𝑥)).
text.formatted: In fact, if we write out the specific distribution of possible rewards in the famous St Petersburg game<ref type="foot" target="#foot_5">foot_5</ref> , we discover that the optimal utility function is almost exactly the function Bernoulli proposed (𝑙𝑜𝑔 (𝑥)).

text.text: Bernoulli's utility function maximizes Pascal's objective for a noisy chooser facing a St Petersburg game-like distribution of possible outcomes.
In contrast, when choosers face a uniformly distributed set of rewards, the optimal utility function is sigmoidal.

The sigmoidal utility function was first widely popularized by Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), but see also Savage and Friedman (Friedman & Savage, 1948) who argued that Bernoulli's function could not account for the behavior of their subjects.
text.formatted: The sigmoidal utility function was first widely popularized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kahneman and Tversky (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)</ref>, but see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Savage and Friedman (Friedman & Savage, 1948)</ref> who argued that Bernoulli's function could not account for the behavior of their subjects.

text.text: One cannot help but note that Kahneman and Tversky performed most of their experiments with environments in which rewards were distributed uniformly.
Environments in which rewards are uniformly distributed, even in the absence of true risk, create a new shape for the utility function that mirrors the one Kahneman and Tversky encountered.
Finally, we found that if choosers face a left-skewed distribution, the optimal utility function is in fact convex.
Choosers in these environments should show a utility structure classically associated with riskseeking behavior.
In traditional economics, this kind of risk-seeking behavior is often referred to as a violation of second-order stochastic dominance.

What this finding suggests is that violations of secondorder stochastic dominance in a left-skewed environment, long treated as irrational, may be much more reasonable than has been generally supposed.
The environments considered here are intentionally simplified.

A natural question is how this environmental sensitivity operates in the real world, where decisions from many different contexts are randomly interleaved and choosers face the hard problem of selecting an estimate of the environment in which they are operating.

While our framework does not include a specific description of how this selection is made, we infer from existing work on this problem that adaptation to the environment is best conceptualized as a slow, implicit process, likely analogous to gain control in sensory systems (Carandini & Heeger, 2012).
text.formatted: While our framework does not include a specific description of how this selection is made, we infer from existing work on this problem that adaptation to the environment is best conceptualized as a slow, implicit process, likely analogous to gain control in sensory systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carandini & Heeger, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In such a specification the utility function reflects a gradually updated approximation to the aggregate reward distribution experienced over the relevant timescale.

This interpretation is consistent with empirical work showing that value representations shift in response to recently encountered reward statistics through mechanisms of range adaptation and divisive normalization (Barretto-García et al., 2023; Khaw et al., 2021; Polanía et al., 2019; Webb, Glimcher & Louie, 2021).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with empirical work showing that value representations shift in response to recently encountered reward statistics through mechanisms of range adaptation and divisive normalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barretto-García et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Khaw et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Polanía et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Webb, Glimcher & Louie, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: How precisely the brain performs this implicit averaging, and over what timescales, remains an important direction for future empirical work and likely is a source of significant inter-individual variation in the selected utility function expressed by different choosers.

Our second class of findings relates to the relationship between cognitive capacity, operationalized as the magnitude of the internal noise in the brain's representation of reward magnitude, and 1) the shape of the utility function and 2) the impact of noise on earnings.
We find that as cognitive capacity increases (or equivalently as internal noise decreases), utility functions in all three straighten.
This is an almost trivial observation.
Pascal demonstrated four centuries ago that a straight utility function was return maximizing for any environment in a chooser with infinite capacity.
This is what we observe.
As noise goes to zero, optimal utility functions shift towards the straight lines Pascal defined as optimal for his noiseless choosers.

What is not trivial is that the nonlinear utility functions that emerge at low to moderate capacity levels are not imperfect approximations to the straight-line ideal but genuinely optimal strategies in their own right.
Much more interesting than this is to examine how reductions in noise change the actual earnings of subjects.
Many hold the intuition that if choosers are very noisy, then they behave randomly and earn very little.
Our findings run against this intuition.

Increases in capacity from 2 to 3, and perhaps even to 4 standard deviations do improve earnings, but much more slowly than one might expect -as long as the chooser is allowed to adapt their utility function to their specific capacity level.
Even more interesting is the observation that above about 4 standard deviations, increases in capacity have very small impacts on overall earnings.
This has, we believe, huge implications for biological choosers.

If one is creating an internal representation of value with a finite biological system that effectively employs just 2 standard deviations in a left-skewed environment, one outperforms a random chooser by 7%.
Doubling the cognitive capacity (roughly doubling the biological cost of the encoding system (Glimcher, 2022)) yields only a 2% additional increment in earnings.
text.formatted: Doubling the cognitive capacity (roughly doubling the biological cost of the encoding system <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Glimcher, 2022)</ref>) yields only a 2% additional increment in earnings.

text.text: What has often been treated as a limitation of biological decision-making systems may instead reflect a rational equilibrium, in which the brain operates at the minimum precision level needed to achieve near-optimal earnings, reserving metabolic resources for other demands.

In Glimcher et al. (2026) we formalize this insight, arguing that choosers or evolution may in fact select a precision level that exactly balances cognitive costs against the benefits of higher precision to maximize their net return optimally.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glimcher et al. (2026)</ref> we formalize this insight, arguing that choosers or evolution may in fact select a precision level that exactly balances cognitive costs against the benefits of higher precision to maximize their net return optimally.

text.text: These results also raise the question of the extent to which human decision makers might intentionally reduce their cognitive costs, reduce their cognitive capacity when in low-stakes environments.
If we think of cognitive costs as being roughly fixed and monotonic, we can assess the degree to which capacity is adjustable by simply repeating the same experiment at different payoff levels.
As we show in some detail in (Glimcher et al., 2026), such experiments could even allow us to determine the cost of capacity and the exact structure of our hidden cognitive cost function.
text.formatted: As we show in some detail in <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Glimcher et al., 2026)</ref>, such experiments could even allow us to determine the cost of capacity and the exact structure of our hidden cognitive cost function.

text.text: Using this approach in the companion paper, we show how an optimal chooser facing a fixed noise cost can select both a capacity and a utility function optimally.
This approach allows us, essentially, to eliminate all free parameters from our model and to treat the selection of an optimal utility function as a fully closed problem.
Recently, significant effort has been devoted to assessing whether human choice behavior can be better thought of as aimed at minimizing errors or maximizing rewards.

Woodford and colleagues (Polanía et al., 2019; Woodford, 2014), amongst others, have tentatively concluded that the two objectives yield such similar optimal choice strategies that it is difficult to empirically resolve this issue.
text.formatted: Woodford and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Polanía et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Woodford, 2014)</ref>, amongst others, have tentatively concluded that the two objectives yield such similar optimal choice strategies that it is difficult to empirically resolve this issue.

text.text: Our data confirm these conclusions in many, but not all, environments.

In uniformly distributed environments, for example, optimal utility functions for maximizing gain and for minimizing errors are almost identical, which might explain why existing experiments have struggled to discriminate between these two objectives.
However, they can be discriminated in bimodally distributed environments, particularly at low capacity levels.
Our data suggest that an appropriately designed environment can be used to experimentally discriminate between these two objectives.
The bulk of the data we present was computed for environments in which there are only 4 possible prizes that lie equally spaced on the objective value axis.
Our fourth general result was developed by examining equally spaced sets of rewards containing more than 4 elements.
While there is no conceptual barrier to selecting sets of any size (or employing any spacing on the value axis), larger sets take more computational time.
For this reason, we limited this presentation to a maximum of 6 possible evenly spaced rewards (See Glimcher et al., 2026, for 7 possible rewards).
text.formatted: For this reason, we limited this presentation to a maximum of 6 possible evenly spaced rewards (See <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glimcher et al., 2026</ref>, for 7 possible rewards).

text.text: As the size of the set of possible rewards grows, the utility functions we encounter become smoother and more classical-looking.
For uniformly distributed rewards, we found that the sigmoidal functions also become steeper and generally look more like the classical value function of Kahneman and Tversky.

Perhaps surprisingly, we found that even left-skewed distributions can yield sigmoidal optimal utility functions, at very low capacities, suggesting that the sigmoid might not be diagnostic of a uniform environment but rather emerges as a universal feature of low-capacity choosers facing sufficiently rich reward sets.
The final result we highlight concerns a variable that has received surprisingly little attention in the utility function literature: the size of the choice set itself.
We found that the optimal utility functions steepen and shift to the right as the size of the choice set grows.
This makes intuitive sense.

As the number of possible draws from the environment increases, the likelihood of encountering at least one option that lies far to the right increases, and the utility function thus shifts to the right to improve accuracy in detecting this best option.
This sensitivity of the optimal utility function to choice set size has not, to our knowledge, been previously presented.
(Although many studies have examined choice set size (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000; Schwartz, 2004; Webb et al., 2021).)
text.formatted: (Although many studies have examined choice set size <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Iyengar & Lepper, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Schwartz, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Webb et al., 2021)</ref>.)

text.text: It should also be noted that these Monte-Carlo-based estimates are not quite as well-behaved as our analytical results.
One will notice immediately that estimates of utility function curvature around reward values that are very rarely encountered in the environment can be somewhat noisy.
This can be seen both in the color plots of all possible utility functions and in the 'best utility function' plots.
This imprecision arises because the Monte-Carlo approach which yields poor estimates of events which are very infrequent.
This can be overcome, of course, by using a much larger number of iterations in the simulations.
Our final general result comes from applying our new framework to an existing dataset in which the same individuals made repeated choices in Uniform and Pareto reward environments.

Unlike standard models in which a utility (or value) function and a noise term are fit by some form of a least squares procedure, to test our model we examine the error matrices produced by our subjects directly and compare them to the error matrices predicted by our theory.
Testing our theory thus resolves empirically to employing a single free parameter and a binomial theorem-based likelihood analysis to assess goodness of fit.
We fit capacity to a subject's observed choice behavior in a three-step process.
First, we explicitly define as an error any choice in which the chooser selects the lower valued option.
Next, we aggregate the pattern of observed errors into an error matrix.
Finally, we compare the empirically observed error matrix to the set of theoretically predicted error matrices which differ in the capacity allocated by the chooser to the choice problem.
We perform this comparison using a simple binomial likelihood procedure.
The result is a best-fit capacity parameter and an overall likelihood score.
The empirical analysis provides two insights into the role of representational capacity in human choice.

First, estimated capacities were strongly correlated across the Uniform and Pareto environments, suggesting that the capacity parameter captures relatively stable individual differences in decision-making precision.
Participants with relatively high capacity in one environment tended to have relatively high capacity in the other.
Second, despite this stability in relative capacity, the estimated levels differed across environments, with participants generally exhibiting lower capacity in the Pareto environment.
Interestingly, this environment also offered lower potential earnings.

One possible interpretation is that choosers adjust the capacity allocated to decision-making in response to the benefits of greater precision, a possibility developed formally in Glimcher et al. (2026).
text.formatted: One possible interpretation is that choosers adjust the capacity allocated to decision-making in response to the benefits of greater precision, a possibility developed formally in <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Glimcher et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: The current results are consistent with this interpretation but do not establish the mechanism underlying capacity allocation.
It is worth noting that models like EU and prospect theory struggle to fit highly stochastic subjects.

For these subjects the utility or value function cannot be well defined because the models rely on their noise terms to account for these choices of these choosers rather than relying on the utility function -thus leading to unspecified utility functions for these choosers.
In our theory, these low-capacity choosers are a key feature of the model.
They are easily and precisely accounted for by our approach.
In contrast, our model struggles to define the precise capacity level of choosers who are nearly perfect expected value maximizers.
This is because these choosers have, in our model, very high-capacity levels.
Whether a chooser has a capacity of 20 or 25 can be hard to distinguish for our model.
Said another way, for these choosers of very high capacity the underlying utility functions are all virtually identical making model fitting difficult.
In contrast, models like expected utility theory and prospect theory can take advantage of this homogeneity because it is the utility function, rather than the capacity, that they are trying to fit.
Finally, we note that all of these differences can make the two classes of models, standard utility models and our capacity model, hard to compare empirically.

The very different fitting procedures, the fact that they can account for different kinds of choosers in different ways, and the different numbers of parameters, all make head-to-head comparisons difficult.
One future direction for our research program will be to develop experiments specifically designed to stress test these models against one another.
The utility analysis presented here has been focused on riskless choice, choices between two certain options.
All theoretical derivations and simulations apply exclusively to this domain.

While many of the utility curves we recover bear striking similarities in shape to those employed by Bernoulli, the Utilitarians of the 19th Century, and Kahneman and Tversky, nearly all of that research was focused on risky-choice and rested on the assumption that the curvature of the utility functions they observed was specifically about a response to risk.

Our finding of essentially identical curvature for the utility function in the absence of risk raises the question of whether a riskless framework can explain phenomena that have traditionally been characterized as specifically related to the domain of risk, a suggestion which builds on recent work by Barretto-García et al. (2023) and Oprea (2024), amongst others.
text.formatted: Our finding of essentially identical curvature for the utility function in the absence of risk raises the question of whether a riskless framework can explain phenomena that have traditionally been characterized as specifically related to the domain of risk, a suggestion which builds on recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Barretto-García et al. (2023)</ref> and Oprea (2024), amongst others.

text.text: The reflection effect is, at its core, a claim about the shape of the utility function around a central reference value.

In 1981, Kahneman and Tversky (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981) described what they referred to as the Reflection Effect, the observation that gambles of equal magnitude above and below the reference point show roughly equal and opposite risk preferences.
text.formatted: In 1981, Kahneman and Tversky <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Tversky & Kahneman, 1981)</ref> described what they referred to as the Reflection Effect, the observation that gambles of equal magnitude above and below the reference point show roughly equal and opposite risk preferences.

text.text: More broadly, this is often taken to imply that for a given chooser, risk attitudes are symmetric but inverted about the reference point.
If the risk attitude above the reference point is modeled as 𝑢(𝑥) = (𝑥 -𝑟𝑝) F , the risk preferences of the same subject can be modeled below the reference point as 𝑢(𝑥) = -(𝑥 -𝑟𝑝) 1F.

While Kahneman and Tversky made this characterization using risky lotteries as the objects of choice, it is of some note that our framework recovers this structure precisely as optimal under specific conditions without any appeal to risk.

As Figure 10F shows, a perfectly symmetrical function can be optimal for a perfectly uniform environment with the inflection point of that sigmoid naturally defining the reference point, but non-uniform environments can require sigmoids that are non-symmetrical.
text.formatted: As Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">10F</ref> shows, a perfectly symmetrical function can be optimal for a perfectly uniform environment with the inflection point of that sigmoid naturally defining the reference point, but non-uniform environments can require sigmoids that are non-symmetrical.

text.text: In our framework, optimality depends critically on both the capacity of the chooser and the distributional structure of the environment and can yield curved cardinal utility functions derived from the patterns of errors a chooser makes, rather than from indifference points amongst the risky lotteries employed by Kahneman and Tversky.

Given this, it seems relevant to note that the actual patterns of observed utility function curvature are highly variable from subject to subject and environment to environment (Bucher & Brandenburger, 2022; Glimcher & Tymula, 2023).
text.formatted: Given this, it seems relevant to note that the actual patterns of observed utility function curvature are highly variable from subject to subject and environment to environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bucher & Brandenburger, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Glimcher & Tymula, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In Chung et al. (2019), we systematically examined utility function curvature in the gain and loss domains and found very little evidence for a reliable reflection of risk attitudes at the single-subject level.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chung et al. (2019)</ref>, we systematically examined utility function curvature in the gain and loss domains and found very little evidence for a reliable reflection of risk attitudes at the single-subject level.

text.text: Only at the population level did we see clear symmetry.
This observed heterogeneity has often led to challenges to the reflection effect.
Under our assumptions, optimality depends on the specific environment encountered by the decision-maker, the decision-maker's beliefs about that environment, and the capacity of the decision-maker.
Another fundamental element of behavioral decision science is Loss Aversion (Kahneman et al., 1991; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), also known as a Gain-Loss Asymmetry (Plott & Zeiler, 2007).
text.formatted: Another fundamental element of behavioral decision science is Loss Aversion <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kahneman et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)</ref>, also known as a Gain-Loss Asymmetry <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Plott & Zeiler, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Where the reflection effect concerns symmetric curvature, loss aversion concerns asymmetric curvature.
In 1979, Kahneman and Tversky noted that human decision-makers were not indifferent between a sure gain of $0 and a lottery which had equal likelihoods of yielding a gain of $10 and a loss of $10.
This was puzzling.
If the human utility function is symmetrical about $0, the equal losses and gains should cancel each other out and choosers should be indifferent between these two options.
Instead, humans show an asymmetry in the assessment of gains and losses under a wide range of conditions.
To understand this phenomena, early prospect theorists made two strong assumptions: First, that the reference point (although unmeasured) was fixed in this experiment at $0.
Second, that the first derivative of the value function above and below the reference point had an identical absolute value (an assumption known as the reflection effect).

Given those two assumptions, the only way to account for these observed phenomena was to hypothesize that "losses loom larger than gains" independent of the curvature of the gain and loss utility functions.

Very important to this analysis, however, are these two assumptions: that the reference point is fixed at a fully-known location and that the utility function has fixed and identical degrees of curvature above and below this reference point.
This immediately raises an important caveat when considering empirical tests of loss aversion.
These tests almost all rely on assumptions about the exact location of the reference point held by the chooser.
To understand this, consider the utility function presented in Figure 10F for an environment with uniformly distributed rewards.
text.formatted: To understand this, consider the utility function presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">10F</ref> for an environment with uniformly distributed rewards.

text.text: By most definitions, the reference point for this function lies midway between 3 and 4.

If an experimentalist were to define 4 as the expected reference point when subjects were using this value function, they would observe a gain-loss asymmetry, a kind of loss aversion: If subjects were given a choice between $4 for sure or a 50/50 chance of either $3 or $5, they would prefer the $4 for sure.
The asymmetry arises because the value function rises more slowly above 4 than it falls below 4.
Were one to repeat the experiment around $3.5, however, the human choice behavior would be perfectly symmetrical and there would be no evidence of loss aversion.
This highlights the importance of an experimentalist's definition of the reference point.
Our data does, however, support the notion that the value function can, under some conditions, be quite asymmetric even in the absence of risky lotteries.
To see this, compare Figures 13F and 13G.
text.formatted: To see this, compare Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">13F</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">13G</ref>.

text.text: While 13F shows a symmetrical function driven by a uniformly distributed environment, 13G shows a highly asymmetrical function driven by a left-skewed environment.

In this construction, however, the loss-gain asymmetry is in no way irrational or puzzling, it is simply a strategy for dealing efficiently with some classes of input distributions and emerges as a feature of decision-makers in the absence of risky lotteries.

Both of these observations suggest that what we call loss aversion can emerge from either a misspecification (by the experimenter) of the reference point, or from an asymmetrical value function driven by the chooser's efficient behavior in a non-uniform environment.
More importantly, perhaps, our approach reveals that loss aversion-like behavior can be observed in the absence of lotteries.
Next, we turn to important extensions to our framework into the domain of truly risky choice.

It is important to note that what follows are speculative extensions of our findings that are not formally derived within the current framework but which we consider to be highly relevant to this work.

While we do adopt a representation of the environment as probabilistic in this paper, it is important to be aware that we do not here include the notion that the object of an actual choice can be, in essence, a lottery ticket.
Extrapolating our approach to prospects that are themselves risky or uncertain requires two additional steps that we have not taken here.
First, we must incorporate the notion of a representation of probability (not just utility) inside the chooser, which is itself cognitively costly and capacity-limited.

If we extend our approach to include the subjective representation of probabilities, we must ask the question: What is the optimal probability weighting function while at the same time asking: what is the optimal utility function?
In a forthcoming presentation we extend our approach to probability weighting functions in this manner.
To address risk in its traditional sense we need to define how choosers should (in a normative sense) represent the environment when it includes probabilistic outcomes.

The critical idea here is that for choosers with limited capacity facing lotteries, there are really two kinds of probability: The probability of encountering a lottery (the environment) and the probability of winning a lottery (the outcome probability).
These two probabilities have different impacts on choice and must be handled separately, which may not be immediately obvious.

One is tempted to bundle these two kinds of probability together: To assume that choosers encode a lottery ticket with a 50% chance of winning $10 as an environment that independently includes both a possible reward of $0 with a probability of 50% and possible reward of $10 with a probability of 50%.

The drawback of such a simple representation is that it entirely neglects the non-independence of these two outcomesthe fact that one cannot choose either the $0 outcome or the $10 outcome but rather that one must choose them together.

To capture the complex non-independence of lottery-like objects one must employ a richer representation of the environment which independently represents these two kinds of probabilities: The probability of encountering a lottery in the environment and the probability of winning that lottery if one selects it.
To study this class of problem using our approach requires an enriched definition of the environment we present in the Methods section.
This enriched definition must capture both kinds of probabilities and any arbitrary covariant structure between offers and lotteries.

Mellers' and Tetlock's classic work (Mellers et al., 2015) on this very problem which examined how different individuals show different degrees of consistency and accuracy in how they use probabilities is a key insight for understanding capacity limits in probability representation.
text.formatted: Mellers' and Tetlock's classic work <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mellers et al., 2015)</ref> on this very problem which examined how different individuals show different degrees of consistency and accuracy in how they use probabilities is a key insight for understanding capacity limits in probability representation.

text.text: Their work reveals that different individuals possess different cognitive capacities for representing probability.
This is a finding very closely aligned with our normative observation that individuals would be expected to employ different cognitive capacities for representing subjective value, or utility.
Our ongoing work in the domain of probability representation rests heavily on these insights.

Both Vieider and colleagues and Maloney and colleagues have completed beautiful work which is also central to the extension of our approach to the domain of risky lotteries (Vieider, 2024; Zhang et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Both Vieider and colleagues and Maloney and colleagues have completed beautiful work which is also central to the extension of our approach to the domain of risky lotteries <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Vieider, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zhang et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Their work examines how decisional accuracy depends on the probabilistic structure of the environment.
This mirrors much of the work we present here, but with a focus more directly on probabilistic representation.
They have devoted significant effort to exploring how distortions of probability might arise as the environmental probability structure is manipulated.
This work also serves as a deep foundation for understanding the optimal representation of probability.
One other key feature of human risk attitudes captured by prospect theory is the so-called four-fold pattern.

Risk attitudes over lotteries depend not just on whether the prospect lies within the gain or loss domain (relative to the reference point) but also depend on the probability of the outcomes under consideration.

Classically, this is presented as four classes of risk attitudes: 1) Risk aversion for high probability gains, 2) Risk seeking for high probability losses, but also 3) Risk seeking for very low probability gains, and 4) Risk aversion for very low probability losses.
The probability weighting function accounts for this phenomenon by overweighting low probability events and underweighting high probability events.

If the four-fold pattern is indeed a robust feature of human choice behavior (a point which is in debate), it is important to note that prospect theory requires the probability weighting function to achieve this pattern specifically because the value function is considered stationary.

In prospect theory, the value function cannot change shape in response to changes in the choice environment and in most experiments, the value of the reference point is treated as fixed for the duration of the experiment.
In the approach we present here, both of these restrictions on the value function have been relaxed.
The shape of the utility function is dependent on both the environment and on cognitive capacity.
The numerical value of the reference point, defined as an inflection in the utility function, also depends on the environment.
While it is not clear from the work we present here whether the four-fold pattern can emerge from these changes, there is some reason to suspect that it might.

When we have previously examined divisive normalization-based models as alternatives to prospect theory (Glimcher & Tymula, 2023), we have found some indication that relaxing these restrictions on the value function may allow a choice system to account for the four-fold pattern without relying on a specific s-shaped distortion of the underlying representation of probability.
text.formatted: When we have previously examined divisive normalization-based models as alternatives to prospect theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Glimcher & Tymula, 2023)</ref>, we have found some indication that relaxing these restrictions on the value function may allow a choice system to account for the four-fold pattern without relying on a specific s-shaped distortion of the underlying representation of probability.

text.text: Traditional theories of decision-making assume that humans possess a fixed utility function that maps objective rewards to subjective value.

From Pascal's expected value to Bernoulli's expected utility theory, they sought to describe how rational agents ought to behave but struggled to reconcile the inconsistencies observed in real human choices.

Modern predictive models such as prospect theory improved the descriptive power of choice theory but largely abandoned normative explanation, leaving unanswered the question of why these irrationalities occur.

In this paper, we propose a normative framework that reconciles these apparent inconsistencies by suggesting that the utility function itself is an adaptive, rational construct shaped by a number of underlying constraints, including environmental statistics and representational precision.

Our framework proposes that the decision-maker, faced with finite representational precision, optimally selects a task-appropriate utility function to maximize long-run average earnings or minimize decision errors for the current environment.

Through analytical derivations and Monte Carlo simulations, we show that the classical utility functions with which all scholars are familiar emerge naturally as optimal encoding strategies under varying environmental and capacity constraints.

Concave utilities optimize performance in environments dominated by frequent small rewards; sigmoidal utilities in uniformly distributed contexts; and convex utilities in environments where large rewards are most common.
As precision increases, these functions converge toward linearity, reflecting a diminishing need for a nonlinear transformation of value in order to optimize the underlying representation.
Further, we quantify the incremental gains from expanding cognitive capacity and find them to be modest once the utility function is optimally adjusted to available capacity.
This finding suggests that bounded rationality may instead reflect a rational equilibrium between computational cost and behavioral efficiency.
The brain, in essence, might well employ the minimal precision necessary to achieve near-optimal earnings given its energetic and informational constraints.

Our findings suggest that when utility is treated as a flexible encoding tool rather than a fixed psychological quantity, bounded rationality becomes not a limitation but an efficient design principle.
The diversity of observed risk attitudes and utility functions across individuals and species can be seen as reflecting an optimal adaptation.
By reframing the utility function as an endogenous, rationally selected encoding mechanism, our framework offers a bridge between prescriptive and descriptive theories of choice.
